sources.title: Tiger Woods' apology: Full transcript
sources.speaker: Tiger Woods (prepared statement at TPC Sawgrass), transcript via CNN
sources.locator: Full transcript, opened and read end to end. Key passages: opening ('always tried to be a private person'); infidelity/entitlement paragraph; 'it's not what you achieve in life that matters'; role-model apology; 45 days inpatient therapy; privacy/children paragraph; Buddhism paragraph; return-to-golf paragraph; closing ask.
sources.excerpt: I want to say to each of you, simply, and directly, I am deeply sorry for my irresponsible and selfish behavior I engaged in. / And while I have always tried to be a private person, there are some things I want to say. / My behavior has caused considerable worry to my business partners. / I was unfaithful. I had affairs. I cheated. What I did is not acceptable. And I am the only person to blame. I stopped living by the core values that I was taught to believe in. I knew my actions were wrong. But I convinced myself that normal rules didn't apply. I never thought about who I was hurting. Instead, I thought only about myself. I ran straight through the boundaries that a married couple should live by. I thought I could get away with whatever I wanted to. I felt that I had worked hard my entire life and deserved to enjoy all the temptations around me. I felt I was entitled. Thanks to money and fame, I didn't have far -- didn't have to go far to find them. I was wrong. I was foolish. I don't get to play by different rules. / I once heard -- and I believe it is true -- it's not what you achieve in life that matters, it is what you overcome. Achievements on the golf course are only part of setting an example. Character and decency are what really count. Parents used to point to me as a role model for their kids. I owe all of those families a special apology. / For 45 days, from the end of December to early February, I was in inpatient therapy, receiving guidance for the issues I'm facing. / I have always tried to maintain a private space for my wife and children. They have been kept separate from my sponsors, my commercial endorsements / Buddhism teaches that a craving for things outside ourselves causes an unhappy and pointless search for security. It teaches me to stop following every impulse and to learn restraint. Obviously, I lost track of what I was taught. / When I do return, I need to make my behavior more respectful of the game. / I ask you to find room in your hearts to one day believe in me again.
sources.context: A scripted, televised statement read to an invited room of friends, staff, sponsors' representatives and pool reporters, with no questions taken. Delivered 84 days after the 2009-11-27 crash outside his home and 79 days after his 2009-12-02 written statement that problems 'shouldn't have to mean public confessions' (S03). The statement was a public-relations event as well as a confession; its self-analysis uses therapy vocabulary. It names no diagnosis: 'the issues I'm facing' is the only treatment language, so any 'sex addiction' label is not established by his words. The Globe and Mail transcript (S02) matches this wording; AJC's live-typed copy is rougher and should not be quoted.

sources.title: Ten years later: players, caddies and observers marvel at Tiger's 2008 U.S. Open win
sources.speaker: Bob Harig (ESPN), oral history quoting Hank Haney, Steve Williams, Rocco Mediate and Tiger Woods
sources.locator: Haney MRI paragraph; Williams paragraph; Tiger's look-back paragraph; Tiger's account of the surgery and fracture (reopened 2026-10-04); final-round and playoff sections
sources.excerpt: Haney: He's explaining about the MRI, it's on his laptop and he's showing there are two stress fractures, as well as the torn ACL. He's showing us everything, but Tiger is not really listening. ... Tiger looks up and says, 'I'm playing the U.S. Open and I'm going to win.' Just like that. Then he says, 'C'mon Hank, let's go practice.' / Williams: I think I asked him on three separate occasions if it was the right thing to carry on. And I got the same reply each time: 'F--- you, Stevie, I'm winning this tournament.' / Tiger: in those four majors, I honestly don't remember missing a putt inside 10 feet. / Tiger: I knew I had to go because I had fragments there, but my surgeons were saying that I also have to have the knee reconstructed. And I said, 'Well, we'll just do a cleanup job first,' because I wanted to play the next three major championships. ... From there, they were saying I was pretty much done for the year. I said, 'Ah, I don't know about that.' / Narration: no one outside of his inner circle knew he was playing with two stress fractures in his tibia ... with an excruciating playoff the next day against Rocco Mediate ... then made the birdie putt to force sudden death after both players shot 71.
sources.context: Oral history ten years after the event. Haney and Williams both later fell out with Woods and wrote books, but here they are admiring rather than critical. Medical facts (torn ACL, two tibial stress fractures, doctors' advice of crutches then rest) are reported widely; Woods himself said on his website after winning that 'the right thing to do is to listen to my doctors' (search snippet only). Reopened during the draft stage on 2026-10-04: the article does not itself state the 'crutches then rest' advice, so the draft uses Woods' own recollection ('they were saying I was pretty much done for the year') instead. It confirms the 18-hole playoff with Rocco Mediate (both shot 71) followed by sudden death.

sources.locator: Body (opened via direct download): 'One of the most guarded athletes' paragraph; speech quotes on parents and earning
sources.excerpt: Lavner: He was slated to talk for seven minutes. But he spoke for nearly 17, without notes or the use of a teleprompter. One of the most guarded athletes in history, here now he was speaking from the heart. / Woods: So without the sacrifices of Mom, who took me to all those junior golf tournaments, and Dad, who's not here, but who instilled in me this work ethic to fight for what I believe in, to chase after my dreams - that nothing's ever going to be given to you, everything's going to be earned. If you don't go out there and put in the work, if you don't go out and put in the effort - one, you're not going to get the results, and two, and more importantly, you don't deserve it. You need to earn it. So that defined my upbringing. That defined my career. / Lavner: For 17 unscripted minutes, Woods made only one passing mention of his life and career this century. Lavner's account includes Woods hiding in 'The Ditch' at the Navy Golf Course, being denied clubhouse access as a junior because of his skin color, and the family's second mortgage, which he paid off with his first Titleist deal. Celebratory setting; memory is 40 years old. The PGA Tour's 2025 obituary attributes 'instilled in me this work ethic' to his mother; Golf Channel's rendering ties it to 'Dad'. Check the video before assigning it to one parent.

sources.title: 2022 World Golf Hall of Fame (March 9) - Tiger Woods

sources.excerpt: My dad, as you have known, is a former special forces and a Green Beret. So mom would drop me off. I would hop into the ditch. I would then walk on the south side of The Ditch because the clubhouse was perched up two stories. ... But dad taught me how to always grab a piece of foliage, cover yourself up, listen for noise. If you hear anybody coming, lay still (laughter). Part sniper. ... at the age of 8, I would play underage the golf course. / I was not allowed in the clubhouses where all the other juniors were. The color of my skin dictated that. As I got older, that drove me even more. So as I was denied access into the clubhouses, that's fine. Put my shoes on here in the parking lot. I asked two questions only, that was it. Where was the 1st tee, and what was the course record. / at the age of 14-1/2 we took out a second mortgage so I could go out and play the AJGA Tour. ... So without the sacrifices of Mom who took me to all those junior golf tournaments, and Dad, who's not here, but who instilled in me this work ethic to fight for what I believe in, chase after my dreams, nothing's ever going to be given to you, everything's going to be earned. If you don't go out there and put in the work, you don't go out and put in the effort, one, you're not going to get the results, but two, and more importantly, you don't deserve it. You need to earn it. So that defined my upbringing. That defined my career, which allowed me to get into a great university like Stanford. / I made practicing so difficult, hurt so much, because I wanted to make sure that I was ready come game time. I hit thousands of balls, hands bleeding, aching, just so that I could play in a tournament. / but in my case, I didn't get here alone. I had unbelievable parents, mentors, friends, who allowed me and supported me in the toughest times, the darkest of times, and celebrated the highest of times. ... This is an individual award, but it's actually a team award. All of you allowed me to get here.
sources.context: Official stenographic transcript of the 2022-03-09 induction speech. Opened directly (raw HTML download) during the draft stage on 2026-10-04 and read end to end; this resolves the research task on wording: the drafted quotes use the ASAP wording, which differs slightly from Golf Channel's rendering (S12), and the 'instilled in me this work ethic' clause refers to 'Dad, who's not here', so the PGA Tour obituary's attribution to his mother is not followed. The Ditch story is told with laughter in a celebratory setting about events roughly 38 years earlier.

sources.title: The Secret History of Tiger Woods
sources.speaker: Wright Thompson (ESPN The Magazine), with named witnesses (John Brown, Ryan Zinke, Billy Helmers, Joe Grohman, Paul Fregia, Michael Jordan) and unnamed friends
sources.locator: Act I: Earl's death and burial; childhood at the Navy Golf Course. Act II: Fort Bragg 2004, SEAL facility 2006, birthday skydive 2006-12-30, Michael Jordan passage, introvert/marketability passage, Halloween text, 'impersonation' and '30 seconds' narration
sources.excerpt: Narration: Seventy-seven minutes after touching down in Kansas, Tiger took off again for Orange County. / Narration: TWENTY-FIVE DAYS after he buried his father and 15 before the 2006 U.S. Open, Tiger went back to visit the Navy SEALs / Brown: 'Why are you here?' ... 'My dad,' Tiger said, explaining that Earl had told him he'd either end up being a golfer or a special operations soldier. / Brown: I definitely think he was searching for something. / Narration: He chose to spend Dec. 30, 2006 -- his 31st birthday -- in San Diego skydiving with SEALs. / Unnamed friend: Frankly, the real Tiger Woods isn't that marketable. There isn't a lot of money to be made off a guy who just wants to be left alone to read a book. / Unnamed friend: Tiger was a natural introvert, and the financial interest for him to be extroverted really drove a wedge in his personality. / Woods (text to Notah Begay about a Halloween costume): I'm going as a golfer known as Tiger Woods. / Narration: Talk to enough people who've met him and it starts to seem like he's doing an impersonation of what he thinks a superstar athlete is supposed to be. / Narration: People who meet him for 30 seconds love him, and people who spend several hours with him think he's aloof and weird, while people who hang around long enough to know him end up both loving him and being oddly protective. / Jordan: He has ... no companion. ... He's gonna have to trust somebody. / Fregia: In some respects, he became what he loathed about his father. / Zinke: Tiger Woods never got wet and sandy. / Narration: Tiger hated that his dad cheated on his mom and cried to his high school girlfriend about it. / Grohman (narration): worried that Tiger didn't have friends his own age until high school. His friends were Earl and Earl's old military buddies.
sources.context: Long-form reported feature (about 18 months), published ten years after Earl's death and after the scandal, so it builds a hindsight narrative. Woods did not participate. Many motive claims come from unnamed friends or SEALs; Brown's 'two paths' account is second-hand recall. 'Impersonation' and the '30 seconds' line are Thompson's narration, not testimony. Fregia was the first director of the Tiger Woods Foundation. Also establishes the birth date (31st birthday on 2006-12-30, so born 1975-12-30) and that Tiger grew up an only child of the marriage with few friends his age (per Navy course pro Joe Grohman).

claims.claim: In his 2010-02-19 statement Woods explained the affairs in his own words: 'I convinced myself that normal rules didn't apply', 'I felt that I had worked hard my entire life and deserved to enjoy all the temptations around me. I felt I was entitled.'
claims.passage: I felt that I had worked hard my entire life and deserved to enjoy all the temptations around me. I felt I was entitled.
claims.inference: His own account links achievement to exemption: a lifetime of earned results bought a private reward and a suspension of rules. 'Convinced myself' is self-deception language. This supports a worth-through-achievement reading (Type 3's self-deceptive image) more than appetite for intensity as such.
claims.alternative: A scripted statement shaped by advisers, therapists and sponsors, with therapy vocabulary; entitlement after fame is common to many celebrities regardless of type. An 8 reading treats the same passage as lust plus rule-defiance. Self-report establishes what he said, not the complete motive.

claims.claim: The same statement reframed his worth from results to character and asked for restored belief: 'it's not what you achieve in life that matters, it is what you overcome. Achievements on the golf course are only part of setting an example', apologized to families who 'used to point to me as a role model', to 'business partners', and closed: 'I ask you to find room in your hearts to one day believe in me again.'
claims.passage: He offered a new measure of worth: "it's not what you achieve in life that matters, it is what you overcome." He ended: "I ask you to find room in your hearts to one day believe in me again."
claims.inference: The repair he sought was in how he was seen: role model, belief, partners. Speaking of image restoration this directly fits a 3's concern with being regarded as valuable.
claims.alternative: Sponsors (Accenture, Gillette, AT&T had dropped or paused him) and an image-based fortune gave commercial reasons to ask for belief whatever his type; crisis PR norms dictate such language.

claims.claim: On 2009-12-02 Woods called privacy 'an important and deep principle' and wrote that 'Personal sins should not require press releases and problems within a family shouldn't have to mean public confessions'; 79 days later he gave a televised confession (2010-02-19).
claims.passage: Five days later he wrote that privacy was "an important and deep principle" and that "Personal sins should not require press releases and problems within a family shouldn't have to mean public confessions"
claims.inference: Observable reversal: privacy was the first defense, then a managed public confession once the image cost grew. Pattern of protecting the public picture first and disclosing on his own terms.
claims.alternative: The reversal can be explained by escalating sponsor pressure, the PGA Tour's interests and advice from crisis managers, not by personality. Strong privacy preference also fits Type 5.

claims.claim: Former American Media CEO David Pecker testified under oath on 2024-04-26 that he bought the 2007 photos of Woods and buried them in return for Woods appearing in Men's Fitness. The draft states there is no public record of Woods' personal role and that his representatives may have made the deal; it does not name the woman photographed.
claims.passage: On April 26, 2024, testifying under oath in an unrelated trial, the publisher's former chief executive, David Pecker, said he had bought the photos and buried them in return for Woods appearing in the magazine
claims.inference: A costly, deliberate image trade: he supplied an idealized public image (fitness and marriage) to keep a contradicting one hidden. This is the clearest observed act of protecting an image rather than confronting a threat.
claims.alternative: Brand protection was worth tens of millions in endorsements, so his agents may have driven the decision; there is no evidence of Woods' personal role or words. Pecker's testimony came 17 years later in an unrelated trial. 'Blackmail' is a reporter's word, not a finding. Sensitive: name the other woman only as reported, if at all.

claims.claim: In his 2017 book Woods wrote: 'I probably came back too early from some of the surgeries, but I was single-minded in my desire to compete and my need for competition.'
claims.passage: "I probably came back too early from some of the surgeries, but I was single-minded in my desire to compete and my need for competition"
claims.inference: He names competing as a need, not just a preference, and accepts physical cost for it. Consistent with identity fused with performance.
claims.alternative: Elite athletes broadly describe competition as a need; career incentives, sponsor obligations and fear of decline explain early returns. Also fits an 8's refusal to yield to the body.

claims.claim: Steve Williams says he asked Woods three times during the 2008 U.S. Open whether to carry on and got 'F--- you, Stevie, I'm winning this tournament' each time.
claims.passage: His caddie, Steve Williams, asked three times whether carrying on was right and got the same reply: "F--- you, Stevie, I'm winning this tournament."
claims.inference: Overriding medical advice and his own caddie to win shows willpower and an extreme priority on winning the biggest events.
claims.alternative: This is the strongest single datum for Type 8 (defiance, dominance, denial of vulnerability). Haney and Williams both later fell out with Woods. Major titles also drove his legacy and earnings. Two witnesses with independent vantage points agree, which strengthens the fact but not the motive.

claims.claim: After winning the 1997 Masters by a record 12 shots, Woods rebuilt his swing; in How I Play Golf (2001) he wrote: 'I didn't see one flaw. I saw about 10 ... by my standard, I felt I had gotten away with murder.'
claims.passage: "I didn't see one flaw. I saw about 10," he wrote in _How I Play Golf_ (2001). "I had struck the ball great that week, but by my standard, I felt I had gotten away with murder."
claims.inference: Accepting a short-term slump after a record win to secure dominance every week. The stated goal is consistent results under pressure, not appearance. Repeated with Haney (2004) and later coaches.
claims.alternative: The perfectionist standard ('by my standard') supports Type 1; the mastery-and-control rationale supports Type 5; the impatience fits 8. A 3 reading has to treat the rebuild as investment in future winning, which is plausible but not unique.

claims.claim: In his 2022-03-09 Hall of Fame speech Woods credited his father ('Dad, who's not here, but who instilled in me this work ethic') with the rule: 'nothing's ever going to be given to you, everything's going to be earned ... you don't deserve it. You need to earn it. So that defined my upbringing. That defined my career' (ASAP Sports wording).
claims.passage: "nothing's ever going to be given to you, everything's going to be earned. If you don't go out there and put in the work, you don't go out and put in the effort, one, you're not going to get the results, but two, and more importantly, you don't deserve it. You need to earn it. So that defined my upbringing. That defined my career"
claims.inference: He states a rule that ties deservingness to earned results, the same logic he used in 2010 to excuse himself ('worked hard ... deserved'). The repetition across 12 years and opposite contexts (confession vs celebration) is the strongest self-report thread for a worth-through-achievement motive.
claims.alternative: This is also a Type 1 moral rule about effort and fairness, and a widely shared athlete ethic shaped by Earl's military values and racial exclusion ('twice as good to be given half a chance', S14). The ASAP transcript (opened 2026-10-04) ties the clause to his father; Golf Channel's rendering differs slightly in wording.

claims.claim: Woods said in 2022: 'I made practicing so difficult, hurt so much, because I wanted to make sure that I was ready come game time. I hit thousands of balls, hands bleeding, aching, just so that I could play in a tournament.'
claims.passage: "I hit thousands of balls, hands bleeding, aching, just so that I could play in a tournament."
claims.inference: Self-imposed pain as preparation; readiness to perform is the organizing value.
claims.alternative: Fits 8 (toughness, pain tolerance), 1 (discipline) and Earl's 'train hard, fight easy' military code as learned practice rather than motive.

claims.claim: At the 2022 Open Woods criticized LIV players: 'they've turned their back on what has allowed them to get to this position' and asked 'what is the incentive to practice? What is the incentive to go out there and earn it in the dirt?' when money is guaranteed.
claims.passage: There he said LIV's players had "turned their back on what has allowed them to get to this position" and asked, "What is the incentive to go out there and earn it in the dirt?"
claims.inference: Same 'earn it' rule as C08, now applied to peers: guaranteed money without earned results is illegitimate. Worth must be earned in competition.
claims.alternative: Woods was a PGA Tour stakeholder and later a Policy Board player director, so institutional interest and loyalty (or Type 6/8 protectiveness of his side) explain the stance too.

claims.claim: An unnamed friend told Wright Thompson: 'the real Tiger Woods isn't that marketable. There isn't a lot of money to be made off a guy who just wants to be left alone to read a book', and another said Woods 'was a natural introvert, and the financial interest for him to be extroverted really drove a wedge in his personality.'
claims.passage: "Frankly, the real Tiger Woods isn't that marketable. There isn't a lot of money to be made off a guy who just wants to be left alone to read a book." Another: "Tiger was a natural introvert, and the financial interest for him to be extroverted really drove a wedge in his personality."
claims.inference: Friends perceive a gap between a commercially produced public self and a private, quieter self. A split between performed image and inner self is central to the Type 3 hypothesis.
claims.alternative: Read straightforwardly, the private self described here (introverted, bookish, wanting to be left alone) is the strongest evidence for Type 5 with a commercially imposed persona. Unnamed sources; hindsight framing.

claims.claim: Asked by Notah Begay about a Halloween costume, Woods texted: 'I'm going as a golfer known as Tiger Woods.'
claims.passage: Woods texted: "I'm going as a golfer known as Tiger Woods."
claims.inference: His own joke treats 'Tiger Woods' as a costume, an awareness that the public figure is a role. Supports the image/self gap in C12.
claims.alternative: Thompson presents it as humor during a hard period. One joke cannot carry a motive claim.

claims.claim: Wright Thompson's narration (2016): talk to enough people who have met Woods 'and it starts to seem like he's doing an impersonation of what he thinks a superstar athlete is supposed to be.'
claims.passage: "it starts to seem like he's doing an impersonation of what he thinks a superstar athlete is supposed to be."
claims.inference: A reporter's synthesis of many interviews: the public persona is rehearsed and modeled on an idea of what a star should be.
claims.alternative: The same aloofness counts against a 3's usual charm and adaptiveness; it fits 5's detachment or 8's indifference to approval. Author narration, not testimony.

claims.claim: Rachel Uchitel said in HBO's 'Tiger' (2021) that Woods 'was sick of trying to hide who he was but he was so scared of the real Tiger not living up to the Tiger that everybody else thinks he is.'
claims.passage: "He was sick of trying to hide who he was but he was so scared of the real Tiger not living up to the Tiger that everybody else thinks he is"
claims.inference: If accurate, this names a fear of the real self failing the public image. That is close to the Type 3 core fear stated in plain language.
claims.alternative: Her interpretation, from a party with an interest in her own rehabilitation; sensitive. Do not lean on it without the independent support of C04, C12 and C13.

claims.claim: After Earl Woods died on 2006-05-03, Woods left Kansas 77 minutes after landing for the burial, visited a SEAL training facility 25 days after the burial and 15 days before the 2006 U.S. Open (where he missed his first major cut as a pro), told a SEAL his reason was 'My dad', and spent his 31st birthday (2006-12-30) skydiving with SEALs.
claims.passage: At the burial in Kansas, Thompson reported, Tiger took off again 77 minutes after landing. Twenty-five days after the burial and 15 days before the U.S. Open, he went back to visit Navy SEAL training. A SEAL, John Brown, asked why he was there. "My dad," Woods said, explaining that Earl had told him he would end up either a golfer or a special operations soldier. Woods missed the cut at that U.S. Open, and he spent his 31st birthday skydiving with SEALs
claims.inference: Grief channeled into his father's world and a dangerous alternative identity, at real career cost (coach objections, a missed cut). It suggests identity searching after losing his primary audience and model.
claims.alternative: This is the strongest behavior the 3 hypothesis does not explain neatly: an arena with no audience and no golf payoff. It fits an 8's appetite for intensity, a 6's identification with his father's code, or grief alone. Zinke says he 'never got wet and sandy', so the training was less immersive than legend says.

claims.claim: Woods described himself in 2006: 'I'm kind of the one who bottles things up a little bit and moves on, tries to deal with things in my own way.'
claims.passage: "I'm kind of the one who bottles things up a little bit and moves on"
claims.inference: Emotion is set aside for function and released only after the result. Consistent with a 3's suspended feelings in service of performance.
claims.alternative: Equally consistent with 5's compartmentalization, 8's guardedness against vulnerability, or Earl's explicit coaching not to let 'emotions get the better of you'.

claims.claim: After Charles P. Pierce's April 1997 GQ profile printed crude jokes Woods told in a limo after a cover shoot, Woods did not deny them; he said he was 'naive about the motives of certain ambitious writers' and objected to 'the attacks on my father'.
claims.passage: Weeks before that first Masters, GQ printed crude jokes the 21-year-old had told in a limousine after a cover shoot. Woods did not deny them. He said he was "naive about the motives of certain ambitious writers" and objected to "the attacks on my father"
claims.inference: An early reputational wound followed by a long era of controlled, bland media access. Protecting image by restricting access.
claims.alternative: Media guardedness is also standard advice for a young star with large endorsements, and fits 5's privacy. The source chain does not prove the GQ episode caused the change.

claims.claim: When Butch Harmon criticized his swing in 2004, Woods said Harmon 'doesn't really know what I'm working on ... and no one knows' and that friends should 'go right up to my face and say it.'
claims.passage: Woods said Harmon "doesn't really know what I'm working on" and added, "If you go say something like that, you go right up to my face and say it"
claims.inference: Secrecy about process and an insistence on private, direct criticism; public loyalty matters.
claims.alternative: The 'say it to my face' code is a classic Type 8 marker; the secrecy fits 5. A 3 reading treats it as protecting his public narrative ('I am close') during a slump, which Harmon called 'denial'.

claims.claim: Butch Harmon said in 2020 that great champions need 'a lot of prick in you' and 'just want to cut your heart out', in remarks framed by Fox Business as describing Woods' mentality.
claims.passage: Butch Harmon said in 2020 that great champions need "a lot of prick in you" and "just want to cut your heart out"
claims.inference: A coach's view that Woods competed with a will to dominate rivals.
claims.alternative: Supports Type 8. Several quotes describe champions in general; the more specific 'win by 10' claim is snippet only.

claims.claim: In Gary Smith's 1996 Sports Illustrated profile, Earl Woods proclaimed: 'He is the Chosen One. He'll have the power to impact nations. Not people. Nations.' Tiger's reported reply ('This is my purpose. It will unfold.') is not used because only an unauthorized reproduction (S56) was opened.
claims.passage: In 1996 Earl told Sports Illustrated: "He is the Chosen One. He'll have the power to impact nations. Not people. Nations."
claims.inference: A parent publicly assigned the child an identity of world-historical achievement. Context for an identity built around performance, not evidence of the son's motive.
claims.alternative: Circumstance, not type: any child framed this way could internalize it. Earl was a self-described mythmaker ('Let the legend grow', S58). Slate (S70) independently quotes the SI line, and GQ 1997 (S26) records Earl's similar 'change the course of humanity' line.

claims.claim: Earl Woods described trying to 'break him down mentally' with distractions during Tiger's swing and ending the training with 'You'll never run into another person as mentally tough as you.'
claims.passage: He described trying to "break him down mentally" with distractions mid-swing, then telling his son, "You'll never run into another person as mentally tough as you"
claims.inference: Earl trained imperviousness to disruption and openly cultivated the legend. Context for later toughness and image management.
claims.alternative: Earl was a self-interested mythmaker ('Let the legend grow'), so his anecdotes may be embellished. This describes the environment, not the son's motive. Do not invent a childhood wound from it.

claims.claim: In 2013, when Charlie was four, Woods said that if his children played golf there would be 'no lessons ... just have fun'.
claims.passage: In 2013, when Charlie was four, he said that if his children played golf there would be "no lessons"
claims.inference: A change of mind: he came to reproduce his father's method, which shows how fully he endorses the training that formed him.
claims.alternative: Could reflect Charlie's own choices and talent rather than Woods' motive. The 2013 account of Earl steering him away from golf conflicts with biographers' accounts.

claims.claim: Woods appeared on national television (The Mike Douglas Show) at age two, in 1978.
claims.passage: He had been in public view far earlier, on _The Mike Douglas Show_ at two, in 1978
claims.inference: He performed for an audience before he could choose to. Context for an identity built around being watched.
claims.alternative: Circumstance alone; a 5 or 8 child could have had the same upbringing. Who arranged the appearance is not documented in opened sources.

claims.claim: Woods said that as a junior 'I was not allowed in the clubhouses where all the other juniors were. The color of my skin dictated that. As I got older, that drove me even more', and that he put his shoes on in the parking lot and asked only where the first tee was and what the course record was.
claims.passage: "I was not allowed in the clubhouses where all the other juniors were. The color of my skin dictated that. As I got older, that drove me even more," Woods said in 2022. He put his shoes on in the parking lot and asked two questions: "Where was the 1st tee, and what was the course record."
claims.inference: Exclusion was converted into fuel for results; results were the answer to status denied.
claims.alternative: Racism is a real, external circumstance; this is resilience under discrimination, not proof of type. Also fits 8's defiance.

claims.claim: At the 2013 Masters Woods said he deliberately dropped 'two yards further back' to take yardage off; the drop was illegal, he was penalized two strokes, and he declined calls (e.g., Nick Faldo's) to withdraw.
claims.passage: At the 2013 Masters, after an illegal drop "2 yards further back" cost him two strokes, he kept playing despite Nick Faldo's call to "sit down and think about this"
claims.inference: Rules were treated pragmatically in service of competing; staying in contention outweighed a gesture of rectitude.
claims.alternative: Counts against Type 1. Withdrawal was not required by the ruling, and many players defended him (Couples).

claims.claim: After his 2017-05-29 DUI arrest in Jupiter, Florida, about seven weeks after spinal fusion surgery, Woods called it 'an unexpected reaction to prescribed medications' and said 'I expect more from myself, too.'
claims.passage: On May 29, 2017, about seven weeks after spinal fusion surgery, Woods was arrested for DUI in Jupiter, Florida. He called it "an unexpected reaction to prescribed medications" and said, "I expect more from myself, too"
claims.inference: Self-managed medication during severe back pain; public framing shifted as facts emerged. 'I expect more from myself' is self-standard language.
claims.alternative: Sensitive medical/legal matter. Chronic pain and surgery are the main circumstantial explanation; this is not type evidence and must not be framed as character diagnosis.

claims.claim: After winning the 2019 Masters, his 15th major, Woods said he had 'serious doubts ... I could barely walk' after 2017 and that he wanted his children 'to see their Pops win, just like my Pops saw me win here', adding 'I wasn't going to let that happen to them twice'.
claims.passage: On April 14, 2019, he won the Masters, his first major since 2008. "I had serious doubts after what transpired a couple years ago. I could barely walk," he said, and he was glad his children could "see their Pops win, just like my Pops saw me win here"
claims.inference: Winning in front of the people who matter to him; the win completes a generational picture.
claims.alternative: Ordinary parental pride; also fits 2/6 belonging motives. Not a discriminator alone.

claims.claim: In November 2021 Woods told Golf Digest a return would be 'never full time, ever again—but pick and choose'.
claims.passage: he said a return would mean "never full time, ever again—but pick and choose"
claims.inference: A stated loosening of identity from competition after near-amputation.
claims.alternative: He nonetheless kept attempting returns (2022-2024 majors, TGL, surgeries in 2024-2025), so behavior partly contradicts the statement; physical limits and business roles explain much.

claims.claim: On 2021-02-23 Woods crashed near Rancho Palos Verdes; the LA County Sheriff said the primary cause was unsafe speed (84-87 mph in a 45 zone). No impairment evidence was found and no citation was issued; Woods said he was 'grateful for all the help I received.'
claims.passage: After a February 23, 2021, crash near Rancho Palos Verdes, California, which the sheriff attributed to unsafe speed, with no evidence of impairment and no citation
claims.inference: His public reply stressed gratitude and recovery, not the speed finding.
claims.alternative: An accident under investigation that found no impairment; no type inference should rest on it.

claims.claim: On 2026-03-27, three days after a TGL appearance, Woods was arrested on suspicion of DUI after a rollover crash on Jupiter Island, Florida; breath test negative; he refused a urine test; the affidavit reported two hydrocodone pills in his pocket.
claims.passage: On March 27, 2026, three days after that TGL match, he was arrested on suspicion of DUI after a rollover crash on Jupiter Island, Florida. His breath test was negative, he refused a urine test, and the arrest affidavit reported two hydrocodone pills in his pocket
claims.inference: A second medication-related driving arrest nine years after 2017, during chronic pain after a seventh back surgery. It tests the career-long pattern of controlled statements and privacy requests.
claims.alternative: Medical and legal facts, not type evidence; pain management and dependence are circumstantial explanations. Plea type conflicts between outlets (no contest vs guilty).
claims.review_trigger: Re-check if Woods returns to competition, makes a substantive public statement about his treatment, faces any further legal matter, or if any outlet corrects the 2026 arrest details.

claims.claim: Woods' 2026 response followed the 2009 pattern of controlled disclosure: a written statement with a privacy request (2026-03-31) and a first public appearance on 2026-06-23, as chair of the PGA Tour Future Competition Committee, that was a prepared statement with no questions. His 2025 statements on his mother's death and his relationship also requested privacy (S43, S44; not detailed in the draft).
claims.passage: What they show is a way of handling exposure unchanged since 2009: a written statement, a request for privacy, and, on June 23, 2026, a first public appearance as chairman of a PGA Tour committee that consisted of a prepared statement and no questions
claims.inference: A stable, decades-long pattern of controlled disclosure on his own terms, from 2009 to 2026.
claims.alternative: Privacy requests are standard for public figures; legal counsel would advise no questions during a pending case. Fits 5 as well as 3.
claims.review_trigger: Re-check when Woods next gives an unscripted interview or press conference, or if his PGA Tour committee or board role changes.

claims.claim: At the 2024 Bob Jones Award Woods said: 'My Mom doesn't get enough credit. They all thought that it was me and Dad on the road, which it was, but Mom was at home.'
claims.passage: "My Mom doesn't get enough credit. They all thought that it was me and Dad on the road, which it was, but Mom was at home"
claims.inference: He corrects the Earl-centred legend of his formation himself.
claims.alternative: Ordinary filial tribute in a memorial context; useful mainly to avoid an Earl-only origin story.

claims.claim: In 2010 Woods said Buddhism 'teaches that a craving for things outside ourselves causes an unhappy and pointless search for security' and 'to stop following every impulse and to learn restraint.'
claims.passage: "Buddhism teaches that a craving for things outside ourselves causes an unhappy and pointless search for security. It teaches me to stop following every impulse and to learn restraint."
claims.inference: His own diagnosis in 2010 is craving for external things and impulse, not image. That cuts somewhat toward the 8 (lust/impulse) or 7 readings.
claims.alternative: The vocabulary is borrowed from Buddhism and therapy. A 3 reading interprets 'things outside ourselves' as external validation, which the text does not specify.

claims.claim: Steve Williams wrote that Woods would 'flippantly toss a club in the general direction of the bag' and had a 'habit of spitting at the hole if he missed a putt'.
claims.passage: Williams wrote that Woods would "flippantly toss a club in the general direction of the bag" and had a "habit of spitting at the hole if he missed a putt"
claims.inference: On-course temper was visible and recognized by Woods himself. Image management was not total.
claims.alternative: Counter to a pure 3 reading (a 3 usually polishes visible conduct); fits 8 or 1 anger. Williams has animus and book incentives, but Woods' own line corroborates the substance.

claims.claim: In his first interviews after the scandal (2010-03-21) Woods spoke of 'stripping away denial and rationalization you start coming to the truth of who you really are' and said of the Masters crowds, 'It would be nice to hear a couple claps here and there.' The disputed 'life of a lie' line is not quoted.
claims.passage: he said therapy meant "stripping away denial and rationalization you start coming to the truth of who you really are," and that at the Masters, "It would be nice to hear a couple claps here and there"
claims.inference: His own framing of the scandal centers on a false life and an unknown true self, and he wants the crowd's approval back.
claims.alternative: Therapy vocabulary from inpatient treatment; wording varies between copies.

claims.claim: Woods said in 2024 that his daughter Sam has 'a negative connotation to the game, because when she was growing up, golf took Daddy away from her.'
claims.passage: Sam has "a negative connotation to the game, because when she was growing up, golf took Daddy away from her"
claims.inference: Names a family cost of his career.
claims.alternative: Ordinary travel cost of a touring athlete.

claims.claim: After Rory McIlroy's 2024 U.S. Open loss Woods said 'We all lose' and 'I still want the last putt', and McIlroy said Woods 'has been nothing but incredible to me'.
claims.passage: Woods said, "We all lose," and McIlroy said Woods "has been nothing but incredible to me." Woods also said: "I still want the last putt."
claims.inference: Late-career mentor warmth alongside an undiminished wish for the decisive moment.
claims.alternative: Mentoring fits many types; the change may be life stage.

claims.claim: Hank Haney said Woods 'wanted to be a Navy SEAL. For sure that was on his list'; agent Mark Steinberg said Haney twisted Woods' 'high respect for the military'.
claims.passage: Haney later said, "He wanted to be a Navy SEAL. For sure that was on his list"; Woods' agent, Mark Steinberg, said Haney had twisted Woods' "high respect for the military"
claims.inference: At his peak, he seriously pursued an identity outside golf tied to his father.
claims.alternative: Contested by his camp; sources have incentives (Haney's book) or are anonymous. Supports the unexplained-behavior column rather than any type.

claims.claim: Michael Jordan told Thompson that Woods has '... no companion' and is 'gonna have to trust somebody'; Paul Fregia said 'In some respects, he became what he loathed about his father.'
claims.passage: Michael Jordan told Thompson that Woods has "no companion" and is "gonna have to trust somebody." Thompson reported that as a teenager Tiger had been upset about his father's infidelity; Paul Fregia, the first director of the Tiger Woods Foundation, said, "In some respects, he became what he loathed about his father."
claims.inference: Friends describe isolation and low trust, and a repetition of his father's infidelity (Thompson reports Tiger cried as a teen about Earl cheating on his mother).
claims.alternative: Friend's speculation and a former employee's view. Low trust fits 5, 6 and 8 as much as 3. Sensitive family material.

claims.claim: At 14 1/2 the family took out a second mortgage so Woods could play the AJGA tour; Golf Channel reported he paid it off with his first Titleist deal.
claims.passage: At 14 1/2, the family took out a second mortgage so he could play the national junior tour; Golf Channel reported that he paid it off with his first Titleist deal.
claims.inference: Loyalty and repayment to family; achievement as provision.
claims.alternative: Fits many types; mainly a humanizing detail.

claims.claim: In his 2017 book Woods wrote of his ex-wife: 'My dishonesty and selfishness caused her intense pain. My regret will last a lifetime.'
claims.passage: "My dishonesty and selfishness caused her intense pain. My regret will last a lifetime."
claims.inference: Sustained ownership of the betrayal seven years later.
claims.alternative: Curated memoir voice.

claims.claim: Eldrick Tont 'Tiger' Woods was born 1975-12-30 in Cypress, California.
claims.passage: Eldrick Tont "Tiger" Woods was born on December 30, 1975, in Cypress, California
claims.inference: Factual metadata.
claims.alternative: Wikipedia is tertiary; the birth date is independently implied by Thompson's report that 2006-12-30 was his 31st birthday (S17). Birthplace rests on Wikipedia only.

claims.claim: In his 2022 Hall of Fame speech Woods recounted sneaking onto the Navy Golf Course at 8 via 'The Ditch', taught by his Green Beret father to 'grab a piece of foliage, cover yourself up, listen for noise. If you hear anybody coming, lay still ... Part sniper', then playing with Earl until dark.
claims.passage: In the Hall of Fame speech, Woods explained how he got onto the Navy Golf Course as an underage 8-year-old. His mother dropped him at the entrance, and he slipped into a ditch on the side the clubhouse couldn't see. His father, "a former special forces and a Green Beret," had "taught me how to always grab a piece of foliage, cover yourself up, listen for noise. If you hear anybody coming, lay still." The room laughed. "Part sniper." When Earl's cart came by after work, they played until dark
claims.inference: A self-told childhood story of hiding unseen until it was time to play; the draft labels the link to his later guardedness as its own reading.
claims.alternative: A humorous anecdote told 38 years later in a celebratory setting; it describes Earl's military habits and a practical way to play underage, not a motive.

claims.claim: Author interpretation: the Ditch story previews a recurring pattern of concealment until performance.
claims.passage: It is a funny story, and an early version of a skill that returns in this profile: staying out of sight until it is time to play.
claims.inference: Thematic link between the childhood anecdote and the later guarded public persona.
claims.alternative: Could be over-reading a funny, practical story; the draft presents it as the profile's framing, not as evidence of type.

claims.claim: Golf Channel reported Woods was slated to speak for seven minutes at the 2022 Hall of Fame induction and spoke for nearly 17, without notes or a teleprompter.
claims.passage: Slated to speak for seven minutes, he spoke for nearly 17, without notes
claims.inference: Sets the unscripted context for the speech quotes.
claims.alternative: Reporter's account; timing approximate ('nearly 17').

claims.claim: Author interpretation linking the 2010 self-justification and the 2022 speech: the same earned-equals-deserving rule.
claims.passage: It is the same rule both times: work earns results, and results make you deserving.
claims.inference: The central thread of the profile: the logic that built the career also supplied the 2010 excuse.
claims.alternative: Shared vocabulary could be coincidence or a common athlete ethic; the 2010 statement was scripted with advisers. The draft keeps both quotes verbatim so readers can judge the parallel.

claims.claim: In the 2010-02-19 statement Woods said: 'I convinced myself that normal rules didn't apply.'
claims.passage: In 2010 it explained an exemption: "I convinced myself that normal rules didn't apply."
claims.inference: Self-deception language tied to the earned-exemption logic of C01.
claims.alternative: Scripted statement with therapy vocabulary; also readable as Eight-style rule defiance.

claims.claim: The draft's type thesis: Type 3 at medium confidence, Type 8 strongest alternative, Type 5 serious second.
claims.passage: Tiger Woods most likely fits Enneagram Type 3, the Achiever, at medium confidence.
claims.inference: Summarizes the type_hypothesis: the deserving rule across contexts plus image repair when picture and private reality diverged.
claims.alternative: Type 8 explains the 2008 U.S. Open, temper and the self-described craving; Type 5 explains the introversion and privacy. Confidence stays medium.

claims.claim: In 2007 Woods appeared on a Men's Fitness cover with a 12-page story about his diet, workout regimen and marriage while the Enquirer's photos went unpublished; the NY Post and WSJ reported the arrangement after the 2009 scandal and American Media denied it at the time.
claims.passage: Woods instead appeared on the cover of Men's Fitness with a 12-page story "about his diet, workout regimen and marriage." The New York Post and The Wall Street Journal reported the arrangement after the 2009 scandal broke, and the Enquirer's publisher denied it
claims.inference: The observable image trade at the center of the Three argument.
claims.alternative: Woods' personal role is undocumented; agents may have arranged it for commercial reasons.

claims.claim: Hank Haney recalls that while the doctor showed the MRI, Woods was 'not really listening' and then said 'I'm playing the U.S. Open and I'm going to win.'
claims.passage: His coach by then, Hank Haney, remembered the doctor showing the MRI while "Tiger is not really listening." Then Woods looked up: "I'm playing the U.S. Open and I'm going to win."
claims.inference: Overriding medical information to pursue a major title.
claims.alternative: Haney later fell out with Woods; recalled ten years on. Strong Type 8 datum.

claims.claim: Before the 2008 U.S. Open, doctors found a torn ACL and two tibial stress fractures; Woods recalled that 'they were saying I was pretty much done for the year' and that he replied 'Ah, I don't know about that.' He had already chosen a cleanup over reconstruction 'because I wanted to play the next three major championships.'
claims.passage: Woods recalled: "From there, they were saying I was pretty much done for the year. I said, 'Ah, I don't know about that.'"
claims.inference: His own account confirms he set aside medical judgment to chase majors.
claims.alternative: Retrospective self-report in an anniversary oral history; consistent with Haney's and Williams' accounts. Fits Type 8 defiance as well as Type 3 priority on titles.

claims.claim: Butch Harmon says he wanted Woods to take a year over the 1997-98 swing rebuild, but 'that's not Tiger Woods. He wanted to do it all right now.'
claims.passage: His coach, Butch Harmon, wanted to go slowly: "But no, that's not Tiger Woods. He wanted to do it all right now."
claims.inference: Impatience for mastery after a record win.
claims.alternative: Decades-later recall; impatience fits Type 8 as readily as Type 3.

claims.claim: Thompson's narration: people who spend several hours with Woods 'think he's aloof and weird', while those who know him long 'end up both loving him and being oddly protective.'
claims.passage: "think he's aloof and weird, while people who hang around long enough to know him end up both loving him and being oddly protective."
claims.inference: Counterevidence to a Three's usual charm up close.
claims.alternative: Reporter's synthesis, not testimony; fits Type 5 detachment or Type 8 indifference.

claims.claim: Golf Channel's Ryan Lavner (2022) called Woods 'one of the most guarded athletes in history'.
claims.passage: He became, in Golf Channel's 2022 phrase, "one of the most guarded athletes in history," though a young star with large endorsements had plenty of reasons to go quiet.
claims.inference: Long-run media guardedness.
claims.alternative: Commercial advice to a young star explains guardedness; causation from the GQ episode is not established, as the draft states.

claims.claim: In 2004 Woods said of his swing work: 'he's never asked me and I've never talked to him about it and no one knows.'
claims.passage: the secrecy about his swing ("no one knows," he said in 2004)
claims.inference: Secrecy about process, cited as Type 5 evidence.
claims.alternative: Protecting a work in progress from a TV critic is ordinary competitive caution.

claims.claim: In July 2006 Woods won the Open at Royal Liverpool, his first major after Earl's death and after his first missed major cut as a pro, broke down, and said 'I wish he could have seen this one last time.'
claims.passage: That July he won the Open at Royal Liverpool, his first major since his father's death and a month after missing his first major cut as a professional. He broke down after the win: "I wish he could have seen this one last time"
claims.inference: Emotion released after the result.
claims.alternative: Ordinary grief; S60 renders the quote differently ('one more time'); the draft uses The Open's wording (S61).

claims.claim: Earl Woods said 'Let the legend grow.'
claims.passage: "Let the legend grow," he said
claims.inference: Earl managed the legend deliberately, a reason to discount his own anecdotes.
claims.alternative: Second-hand through a 2006 obituary feature; describes Earl, not Tiger's motive.

claims.claim: In December 2022 Woods described testing his son Charlie with Earl-style mental pressure: 'if I can get into his head, that means someone else can get in his head ... That's what my dad believed in. You've got to be willing to take it.'
claims.passage: By December 2022 he was testing Charlie the way Earl had tested him: "if I can get into his head, that means someone else can get in his head. ... That's what my dad believed in. You've got to be willing to take it."
claims.inference: A change of mind from 2013's 'no lessons': he came to reproduce his father's method.
claims.alternative: May reflect Charlie's own choices and talent rather than Woods' motive.

claims.claim: The 2017 toxicology report found five drugs (hydrocodone, hydromorphone, alprazolam, zolpidem, THC); Woods said in August 2017 'it was a mistake to do this without medical assistance' and pleaded guilty to reckless driving through a diversion program in October 2017.
claims.passage: Toxicology found five drugs, including painkillers, sleep medication and THC. He later called it "a mistake to do this without medical assistance" and pleaded guilty to reckless driving
claims.inference: Self-managed medication during severe back pain.

type_hypothesis.against: Several strong observations resist a Type 3 reading. (1) Peers and reporters find him aloof, cold and uninterested in being liked by most people (C14, C44), and he let on-course temper, club-tossing and spitting damage his image for years (C38). A 3 usually polishes visible conduct and charms. (2) Friends describe the private Woods as a natural introvert who wants to be left alone with a book (C12), which reads naturally as a Type 5 core behind a commercially imposed persona. (3) His defiance and will to dominate (playing the 2008 U.S. Open on a broken leg against doctors' advice and telling his caddie 'F--- you, Stevie', C06; Harmon's 'prick' mentality, C20; 'say it to my face', C19) and his appetite and impulse in 2009 (C01, C37) fit Type 8, whose passion is lust; his own 2010 Buddhist diagnosis names craving and impulse, not image (C37). (4) After 2021 he repeatedly risked public failure in diminished comebacks (C31), the exposure a 3 is said to avoid. (5) Much of his image control has a commercial explanation: endorsements dwarfed prize money, and his agents may have made the 2007 Enquirer deal (C04). (6) The moral rules ('you don't deserve it', 'I expect more from myself', 'core values', C08, C29, C01) and swing perfectionism ('by my standard', C07) give a Type 1 reading some support. (7) Being proclaimed 'the Chosen One' and on national TV at two (C21, C25) is circumstance that could produce a performance-centred identity in any type.
type_hypothesis.alternative_case: Type 8 is the strongest alternative. It explains overriding his doctors and caddie to win the 2008 U.S. Open on a torn ACL and two stress fractures (C06), the intimidation and desire to crush rivals that coaches describe (C20), his self-imposed painful practice (C09), the face-to-face loyalty code and secrecy toward his old coach (C19), the denial of vulnerability ('bottles things up', C17), the excess and impulse of the 2009 affairs that he himself framed as craving (C01, C37), the risk-seeking SEAL training (C16, C43), visible temper on the course (C38), and fierce protection of his family and institution (C03, C10). Type 5 is a serious second alternative: the introvert friends describe (C12), lifelong privacy and secrecy about his process (C03, C19, C35), compartmentalization (C17), an adult and military childhood world with few peers (C17 source S17), and low trust (C44). Type 1 is a weaker third: standards, 'core values', 'I expect more from myself' and swing perfectionism (C07, C08, C29), but it fails against 'I convinced myself that normal rules didn't apply' (C01) and the pragmatic 2013 drop (C28).
type_hypothesis.discriminator: What he does when the public picture and the private reality diverge. Across decades Woods' characteristic move is to manage the picture, not to own the appetite openly (the 8 pattern) or to withdraw from public exposure (the 5 pattern). In 2007 his side supplied an idealized fitness-and-marriage cover story so contradicting photos stayed buried (C04, C56, C88; Pecker's sworn 2024 testimony). In 2009 he invoked privacy as principle, then gave a televised confession that cited worry to business partners, apologized to parents who used him as a role model and asked the public to 'believe in me again' (C02, C03, C87). His private self-justification was that earned results bought exemption: 'worked hard my entire life and deserved ... I felt I was entitled' (C01, C54). The same earned-equals-deserving rule recurs in contexts with different incentives: 'need for competition' in 2017 (C05), 'you don't deserve it ... You need to earn it ... That defined my career' in 2022, attributed to his father in the ASAP transcript (C08), and 'earn it in the dirt' against LIV in 2022 (C10); the draft states the parallel as interpretation (C53, C79). Friends describe the public figure as a role he performs ('a golfer known as Tiger Woods', 'impersonation', the real one 'isn't that marketable', C12-C14) and a former partner says he feared 'the real Tiger not living up to the Tiger that everybody else thinks he is' (C15). An 8 is not usually troubled by a gap between persona and self and does not ask to be believed in again. A 5 minimizes appetite and public spectacle rather than seeking the largest stage (C81). Commercial incentive explains brand protection, but not as clearly the private 2010 self-justification or the 2022 moral rule about deserving. The 8 explanation must still answer C06, C57, C58 and C20, so confidence stays medium. (Revised at draft: Tiger's 1996 'This is my purpose' line was dropped because only an unauthorized reproduction was opened; C21 now carries only Earl's corroborated prophecy, which is circumstance rather than discriminator evidence.)
type_hypothesis.unexplained: The Navy SEAL pursuit at his peak and in the months after his father's death (C16, C43, C74): a dangerous, audience-less identity tied to Earl that cost him at the 2006 U.S. Open and has no golf payoff. The bookish homebody friends describe beside the Las Vegas nights. Coldness toward people whose admiration a 3 would court (C44, C60), and on-course temper he let damage his image (C38, C73). His late-career warmth as a mentor and his tears at the Hall of Fame (C41, S12) beside lifelong guardedness. The shift from 'no lessons' to Earl-style mental tests with his son (C24, C65). Becoming, in a former foundation director's words, what he loathed in his father (C44). The 2017 and 2026 medication-related driving arrests (C29, C34) are best explained by chronic pain after repeated spinal surgery and are not type evidence.
